analysis.one_liner: Bases Medicare Part D drug coinsurance on the drug's discounted net price instead of its inflated list price.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 1, 2024 with one bipartisan cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a Medicare drug plan charges patients a percentage of a drug's price, it currently uses the list price — the sticker price before the discounts manufacturers give in secret negotiations. Because those discounts are large, patients paying 25% of the list price can pay far more than the drug actually costs. This bill would require plans to calculate that coinsurance using the net price — the price after manufacturer discounts — so seniors' cost-sharing falls when the real price falls.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D beneficiaries who pay coinsurance (a percentage of a drug's price) for brand-name drugs between their annual deductible and the out-of-pocket cap. Their out-of-pocket drug costs would drop because the percentage would be applied to the discounted net price rather than the higher list price. Low-income seniors and those on fixed incomes taking expensive brand-name drugs would benefit most.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that for plan years beginning 2025 or later, coinsurance for covered Part D drugs be calculated on the drug's net price rather than its list price, whenever the net price is lower [S2].
Defines net price as the negotiated plan price net of manufacturer-provided price concessions, as reported in the plan's Detailed DIR Report [S2].
The sponsor, Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-NV), introduced the bill with Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX), giving it bipartisan sponsorship [S1][S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers, whose combined list-price-minus-net-price spread is partly paid by patients through list-price-based coinsurance. Insurers offering Part D plans would face added reporting and plan-design adjustments. Plans could respond by raising premiums or shifting to flat copays.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug manufacturers, PBMs, and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: The requirement only applies to costs between the annual deductible and the annual out-of-pocket threshold, and it explicitly excludes drugs described in paragraphs (8) and (9) of the statute, so a portion of beneficiaries' drug costs would still be based on list price [S2].
The net price is taken from the previous plan year's Detailed DIR Report, so coinsurance would be based on year-old negotiated prices, which may lag actual current prices [S2].
Plans could respond by replacing coinsurance with flat copays or changing formularies, which could blunt the benefit for some patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core fix is sound: charging seniors a percentage of a fictional list price when the drug's real price is much lower overcharges them. The bill is narrow — it does not apply above the out-of-pocket cap, excludes some drug categories, and uses prior-year price reports — so its reach is limited, but for the patients it covers the benefit is direct and the cost falls mostly on manufacturers and intermediaries who currently benefit from the list-price gap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 1, 2024 by Sen. Rosen, for herself and Sen. Cornyn [S2][S4].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, floor vote, or companion House bill — appears in the action history before the Congress ended January 3, 2025 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers keep the list-price-based coinsurance structure that shifts part of their rebate spread onto seniors' out-of-pocket costs; no senior saw a change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers and PBMs kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Jacky Rosen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 1, 2024, for herself and Sen. Cornyn.

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor, making it a bipartisan introduction.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 1, 2024 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; no further action appears before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but it never advanced far enough for a partisan split to appear; its death reflects committee inaction, not a roll call.

industries.note: Manufacturers negotiate large confidential rebates so the net price is well below the list price; when patient coinsurance is figured on the list price, part of that gap lands on seniors. Basing coinsurance on net price would cut that revenue channel.

PBMs help set the negotiated net prices and concessions reported in the Detailed DIR Report; the current structure obscures the spread between list and net price. Net-price-based coinsurance makes the discount flow through to patients instead.

industries.industry: Part D prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage drug plans
industries.note: Plans would have to compute cost-sharing from reported net prices and could face pressure to adjust premiums, copays, or formularies to offset the change.
